title: Strands Decider MCP Explained for Agent Builders
summary: Strands Decider MCP isn't a real product—the term joins two distinct technologies: Strands Agents (AWS's SDK) and MCP, the agent-to-tools protocol.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces as an MCP Server for Strands Agents


When a Strands agent must act inside business apps, Activepieces fits: each of its 750 integrations is already a tool on a per-project MCP server, under an MIT-licensed core. It doesn't replace Strands, and it doesn't supply a "decider."


### What the agent gets and what stays in the workflow


From the agent's side there is only a tool with a name and inputs. Behind it sits a fixed sequence that someone reviewed.


The recovery path, the branch on failure and the human sign-off are written into the workflow, so they're not improvised by the model at run time. That answers the risk from the previous section: the error policy becomes a reviewed artifact instead of an inference.


### An example workflow


Picture the pattern on Activepieces' homepage. A lead arrives from HubSpot, the customer-relationship system that triggers the flow. An AI step qualifies it, a condition branches on the result, and only then do the Salesforce record, the Slack notification and the Gmail send run.


Look at the "Custom Logic" tab, which is selected in that view: the model makes one bounded judgment, and everything with side effects sits behind explicit steps.


A run is 1 credit however many steps it has, and the AI step costs 2 credits on a fast model.


### Who owns what


In practice, the tool's audit trail lives in the workflow's run history, not in your agent's prompt. Strands still owns the conversation, the model choice and the decision to call the tool.


Activepieces owns what happens once the call lands, because a piece connected there is already a tool on its per-project MCP server. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties all run Activepieces.


That holds for each of its 750 integrations, and none of them needs a second registration for your Strands agent: the integration action that runs as a step in a flow is the same one exposed as an MCP tool, which you can confirm in packages/integrations in the open source repo, so once configured, an integration is available to you in both contexts without additional setup.


A catalog you would have to re-integrate for agents is a second migration, and this one isn't. The workflow holds the credentials, so whoever edits it controls what the agent can reach.


### Check the vendor's terms


Confirm the current MCP behavior in[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) ' own MCP documentation and its pricing page before you rely on either. As of that page's 2026-10-23 check, MCPs are included on the free plan, which gives 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows.


Plan terms for approvals and run history are the vendor's to state, not this article's.


### When a direct tool is the better choice


When the action is a single call to an API you control, a direct Strands tool is the better choice. It suits actions with no side effects that need sign-off and no need for a non-engineer to change them.


Adding a workflow layer there adds a second system to monitor, a second set of credentials and another place for failures to hide.


Choose Activepieces when a step needs a human approval or a multi-app sequence; flows are unlimited on every plan, including free. Choose a direct tool when the logic is small enough to read in a single function.
